inputs.text: [serious] Sixty-six million years ago, [pauses] at the end of the Cretaceous. For a long time now, the Earth has been rumbling.
[curious] Rumbling how?

[serious] In India, giant volcanoes spit out lava, [pauses] smoke, and ash. [gasps] The ground splits open for miles, and lava shoots out of the cracks. [calm] Earthquakes shake the land [softly] and scare the animals. [pauses] The sky is already gray.
[nervous] Are the dinosaurs still alive?
[warmly] They are. [softly] The sun still shines through. [calm] Triceratops munches, T. rex hunts, life goes on.
[curious] And then?

[whispers] But one day... [pauses] far away in the sky, a tiny dot shines. [serious] The dot gets closer... [nervous] it gets bigger... [gasps] bigger still... [excited] it's huge, it's burning, it's whistling, it's racing toward the Earth... [shouts] AND SUDDENLY: a GIANT meteorite falls from the sky! [amazed] Six miles wide: as wide as a whole city, [pauses] or a hundred football fields in a row.
[gasps] Where does it land?

[serious] In Mexico, [pauses] on the Yucatán peninsula, in a shallow sea. [gasps] It digs a hole a hundred and ten miles wide: the Chicxulub crater. [softly] Even today, it sits half on land and half under the sea.
[curious] It just makes a big hole. Is that really so bad?

[serious] At the moment of impact... [pauses] a terrible heat. [nervous] It spreads... [serious] it flattens the trees... [gasps] it burns the forests... [shouts] more than SIX HUNDRED MILES away, everything is swept away or burned in seconds! [serious] The Earth shakes like never before: [pauses] in the mountains, chunks of rock crumble away, [softly] and whole forests fall.
[nervous] And in the sea?

[serious] Giant waves. [nervous] They rise... [gasps] and rise again... [shouts] near the crater, taller than a THIRTY-story building! [pauses] Far away, on oceans all over the world, they're still three stories tall, [serious] and they crash over every shore. [softly] And tons of dirt and dust keep rising into the sky.
[curious] Why do you keep talking about the sky?
[softly] Because on land and in the sea, it's terrible: [sad] thousands of hurt animals, [pauses] many who die. [serious] But that's not the worst. [pauses] The real disaster is up in the sky.
[nervous] Does it turn black?
[whispers] All black. [pauses] For days... [softly] for months... [gasps] probably for YEARS. [calm] No sun, no light, no warmth. [softly] It gets cold, colder and colder.
[curious] Who dies first?

[sad] The plants. Without sunlight, plants die, [pauses] and the food chain breaks. [softly] The big plant-eaters have nothing left to eat, and they starve. [serious] Then the meat-eaters, [pauses] one after another, die too.
[sad] Triceratops too?
[softly] Triceratops too. [serious] On land, everything bigger than a big dog is gone. [pauses] All the dinosaurs die.
[curious] Is anyone left?
[warmly] The small ones, [pauses] quick and tough: little mammals, little birds, [happily] and birds are real dinosaurs. [calm] In the sea too: sharks, turtles, crocodiles.
[curious] Is that the end?

[serious] It's the end of the Cretaceous, [pauses] and the end of the Mesozoic, the age of the dinosaurs. [calm] Scientists call this moment the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary. [warmly] Because with this great extinction, a new era begins: [pauses] the Cenozoic, with its first period, the Paleogene. [happily] And when the sky clears, [pauses] it's the little ones' turn.
